title: An ignition-delay panel asks: does the tuned mechanism pass through the data where the nominal one does not?
summary: Each panel plots ignition delay on a log axis against 1000/T for one fixed mixture and pressure. Three things share the axes: the nominal mechanism, the tuned mechanism and the experiments with their error bars. The reading is a comparison of distances to the data, condition by condition.

media.alt: Three panels of ignition delay in milliseconds on a log axis against 1000/T. Left: n-heptane, phi 1, P 42, two points where the nominal line sits above the experiment and the tuned line is closer but still above. Middle and right: 1,3-butadiene at phi 1 P 40 and phi 2 P 20, six points each, where nominal and tuned lines run close together near the experimental points.

read_the_figure.question: For each operating condition (equivalence ratio phi and pressure P), is the tuned mechanism closer to the measured ignition delays than the nominal mechanism is?
read_the_figure.axes: x: 1000/T in 1/K, so temperature falls to the right. y: ignition delay in milliseconds on a logarithmic axis. Each panel is one condition, given in its label box (phi and P). Legend: grey dashed line with squares is the nominal mechanism, orange line with triangles is the best tuned fit, blue open circles with bars are the experiments with a plus or minus 10 percent bar.
look_at: Pick one panel and ask first whether the experimental bars lie close to the straight line a thermal-activation (Arrhenius) law would draw. A roughly straight run of points is normal chemistry; a bend or flat stretch is a change of the dominant chemistry with temperature.

Measure the vertical gap between each line and each blue circle. On a log axis equal vertical gaps are equal relative errors, so gaps can be compared between panels with very different delay magnitudes.
Check whether the orange line enters the error bar. A line within the bar is as good as the measurement can say.
Look for panels where the two lines nearly coincide: there the tuning changed very little, and for those conditions the objective had nothing to gain.

In the grids look for panels with only two points (little can be concluded) and for panels with two or more separate lines, which are different mixtures or data sets drawn in one panel. The one methyl-butanoate panel at phi 1 and 30 atm lies at much lower temperature than the rest (its x range is near 1.1 to 1.2) and is the place where both mechanisms visibly miss the trend.
read_the_figure.proves: If, panel after panel, the orange line is nearer the circles than the grey line, the tuned parameters improve the agreement with data that were part of the objective. It does not by itself show that the mechanism predicts conditions that were not used: that needs held-out conditions.
if_wrong: A panel where the orange line is farther from the data than the grey line: tuning improved the aggregate objective at the expense of this condition. The aggregate score hides such trade-offs.

Both lines far from the data in one panel while the others agree: that condition is an outlier, either in the mechanism (missing chemistry in that regime) or in the experiment. The log axis makes a factor-of-two miss look modest, so read the axis values.
Lines that are straight while the data bend: the model does not reproduce a change of regime with temperature, even if it matches at the ends.
A panel with only two or three points: a line drawn through so few points proves little. The caption of the larger panel grids says how many conditions and points survive.
must_check: The y axis is logarithmic and labelled with its unit.
The experimental uncertainty is drawn, and its stated size (here plus or minus 10 percent) is in the legend.
Both models appear in every panel, with the same marker and line style throughout.
The x range of each panel is different; do not compare slopes by eye between panels without checking the scales.
The number of conditions shown, and how many were dropped, is stated (the grid titles say 'N of M target datasets survive').

terms.meaning: The time from the start of the experiment (typically after the shock or compression that heats the mixture) until ignition is detected. Plotted in milliseconds.
The fuel-to-oxidizer ratio relative to the exact stoichiometric ratio. Below 1 is lean, above 1 is rich.
A plot of the logarithm of a rate-like quantity against 1/T. A thermally activated process is a straight line whose slope is proportional to the activation energy.
The reaction mechanism with its published rate parameters before any tuning. It is the baseline against which the tuned fit is judged.
The same mechanism with selected rate parameters changed within their allowed uncertainty so that the predicted delays match the experiments better.
The experimental uncertainty. A model line that passes through the bar agrees with the measurement as far as the measurement can tell.
The miss divided by the measured value. On a log axis it is, for small values, the same as the vertical gap in ln of the delay.

remember: Ignition delay is plotted as ln tau against 1000/T because thermally activated chemistry is then a straight line.
On a log axis, equal vertical gaps are equal relative errors.
Tuning can improve the aggregate and worsen individual conditions: read the panels, not just the total.
Agreement with the conditions used in the fit is not prediction of new conditions.
A bend or flat stretch in the data means a change of dominant chemistry with temperature.

understand.title: Why the panels are separate
understand.text: Ignition delay depends strongly on mixture and pressure. Putting every condition on one set of axes would hide small misses behind large spreads, so each condition has its own panel and its own scale, which also means the scales differ from panel to panel.

understand.title: Why 1000/T
understand.text: The Arrhenius form makes the logarithm of the delay linear in 1/T. Multiplying by 1000 only makes the tick labels convenient numbers near one.

understand.title: Representative panel versus full grid
understand.text: The representative figure shows three conditions chosen to illustrate the comparison. The three companion figures show every condition of one fuel, one panel each: 12 conditions for n-heptane, 7 for methyl butanoate and 9 for 1,3-butadiene. Their titles state how many of the target data sets survive the merge, so the full grids also show how much of the original data set was kept. They are the honest version of the representative figure, because the poor panels are included.

steps.title: An activated delay is a straight line in 1/T
steps.note: This is the standard Arrhenius form with an apparent activation energy for the whole ignition process. The slope of a panel is therefore a measure of an apparent activation energy; it is not the activation energy of any single reaction.

steps.title: Slope in the units of the figure
steps.note: With x equal to 1000 over T in kelvin, the slope of ln tau against x is the apparent activation energy divided by 1000 R. Steeper means more sensitive to temperature.

steps.title: Equal vertical gaps are equal relative errors
steps.note: The signed relative error is the model minus experiment, divided by experiment. For small values, it equals the gap on a log axis. This is why the figure uses a logarithmic axis.

steps.title: What a plus or minus 10 percent bar looks like on a log axis
steps.note: The bar is nearly symmetric: about 0.04 decades each way. On a panel spanning a decade this is a small bar, and a model line outside it is more than 10 percent off.

steps.title: The score behind the picture
steps.note: The mean relative error over the N points of a panel (or over all panels, with weights). The picture lets you see which points supply the total, which the single number cannot.

worked.title: Relative error and log gap for one read-off point
worked.problem: In the n-heptane panel at phi = 1 and P = 42, read the tuned line near 0.30 ms and the experiment near 0.26 ms (read by eye, about 10 percent). What are the relative error and the gap on the log axis?

solution.text: Relative error of the model against the experiment.
Gap in natural-log units, for comparison.

worked.answer: About 15 percent, or 0.14 in ln units: for these sizes the two measures agree to within about 10 percent of each other, which is why the log gap is a fair reading of the relative error. The error bar is plus or minus 10 percent, so the line is just outside it.

analyze.q: In a panel the tuned line is below the nominal line, and both are above the data. Has tuning helped? What would you need to know?
analyze.hint: The distance to the data, not the direction of the move.

analyze.q: One panel has the nominal and tuned lines almost on top of each other. List two reasons this can happen.
analyze.hint: Insensitivity of that condition to the tuned parameters; or the objective gave it little weight.

analyze.q: Why can a mechanism that fits every panel in the grid still fail on a new condition?
analyze.hint: Fit versus prediction; overlapping parameters; regimes that were not sampled.

evaluate.q: Is the plus or minus 10 percent bar adequate to claim agreement, given that the model parameters were tuned to these same points?
evaluate.hint: Think of overfitting and of the true experimental scatter.

evaluate.q: The representative panels were chosen from a larger grid. What bias could the choice introduce, and how does the full grid fix it?
evaluate.hint: Selection of illustrative cases; the full grid shows all conditions, including the poor ones.

create: Redesign the panel grid so that each panel also shows the signed relative error in a thin strip below it, with the 10 percent band shaded.
Design a hold-out test: which conditions would you remove from the fit, and what would you plot to show prediction instead of fit?

checks.q: Why is the vertical axis logarithmic?
checks.hint: Delays span decades and the physics is exponential in 1/T.
checks.answer: Because the delay changes by orders of magnitude and because thermally activated chemistry is a straight line on ln tau against 1/T. It also makes equal vertical gaps equal relative errors.

checks.q: A model gives 0.55 ms where the experiment gives 0.50 ms. What is the relative error?
checks.hint: Divide the miss by the measurement.
checks.answer: (0.55 - 0.50) / 0.50 = 0.10, that is 10 percent, at the edge of a plus or minus 10 percent error bar.

checks.q: The data in a panel bend, but both model lines are straight. What does this say?
checks.hint: A bend is a change of apparent activation energy.
checks.answer: The models do not capture a change in the dominant chemistry with temperature. They can match at the ends of the range and still miss in between.

checks.q: Tuned is closer to data in 10 of 12 panels and farther in 2. Is the tuning successful?
checks.answer: On the whole yes, but the two panels where it got worse need explaining: they can mark a conflict between conditions that the parameters cannot resolve, or an outlying experiment.

checks.q: What extra panel would show whether the improvement transfers to a new pressure?
checks.hint: A condition that was not in the objective.
checks.answer: A held-out condition (a pressure or equivalence ratio not used in the fit) drawn with the same legend, showing nominal, tuned, and experiment.
